analysis.one_liner: Lets the Justice Department recover and cap outsized executive pay at companies that took big federal bailouts.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared committee but failed on the House floor, 223-196 — it needed a two-thirds majority, and 165 of 178 Republicans voted no.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that received more than $10 billion in federal bailout money after September 2008 would have faced two new rules. First, the Justice Department could sue to claw back executive pay that was excessive, treating it like an illegal transfer away from a company that was effectively broke. Second, no executive at such a company could be paid more than 10 times the average pay of the company's non-management workers. The bill gave the Attorney General subpoena power to investigate compensation contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the bailouts, since the Justice Department could recover pay executives received from companies that were kept alive with federal money. Workers at those companies also benefited from the cap tying top executive pay to the pay of average employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and employees of bailed-out firms

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the Attorney General to sue in federal court to recover compensation paid by a bailout recipient that received less than a reasonably equivalent value in exchange, when the company was insolvent apart from the federal money it received [S2][S3][S4].
Caps compensation at recipient companies at 10 times the mean pay of the company's nonmanagement employees, enforceable through a Justice Department civil action [S2][S3][S4].
Gives the Attorney General subpoena power over witnesses and documents, including the circumstances of employment contracts and compensation payments, enforceable by court order [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Executives and shareholders of the large companies that took more than $10 billion in federal assistance — including major banks and auto companies — who could see past pay clawed back and future top pay limited to 10 times the average worker's pay.

drawbacks.text: The bill applied retroactively to payments made after September 1, 2008, and Congress invoked its bankruptcy power explicitly to try to support that reach — a sign that its legal footing for clawing back already-paid compensation was contested [S3][S4].

The 10-times-average pay cap is a blunt instrument: it applies to every company above the $10 billion threshold regardless of circumstances, and supporters of executive pay flexibility would argue it could complicate retaining leadership at firms already in distress [S2][S4].

The bill's scope was limited to firms that took more than $10 billion in federal assistance and companies that were insolvent apart from that aid, so excessive pay at firms just under the threshold or on stronger footing would not be touched [S2][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real and widely resented problem: companies that survived only because taxpayers kept them solvent paying their executives large sums anyway. Recovering that pay and tying future top pay to the average worker's pay would have directly recaptured public money and changed incentives. The costs are the legal fragility of retroactive clawbacks and the bluntness of a one-size-fits-all pay ratio. On balance it was a taxpayer-protection measure whose main cost fell on a small group of highly paid executives at bailout recipients.

outcome.mechanism: The House brought it to the floor under a fast-track procedure that requires a two-thirds majority, and it failed 223-196, with Republicans voting nearly unanimously against it; the Senate never took it up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2009 and the House Judiciary Committee marked it up the next day, reporting it by voice vote on March 24 [S6].
On April 1, 2009, the House considered the bill under suspension of the rules, a procedure that requires a two-thirds majority to pass, and the motion failed 223-196 (Roll no. 178) [S7].
214 of 253 House Democrats voted yes and 9 of 178 Republicans voted yes, so the bill fell short largely on party lines [S7].
The bill received no further action in the House and was never considered by the Senate before the Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of the large companies that received more than $10 billion in federal bailout money are better off: no past compensation was clawed back and no cap was imposed on future pay. The financial industry also avoided a Justice Department mechanism for reviewing executive compensation contracts.

industries.industry: Executives at large federal bailout recipients (major banks, AIG, and the auto companies)
industries.note: The bill would have let the Justice Department claw back compensation these executives received while their companies were insolvent apart from federal aid, and capped future top pay at 10 times average worker pay. Their interest in blocking it ran directly against recovering taxpayer money.

Firms that took more than $10 billion in federal assistance faced government review of their employment contracts and a pay cap, and the industry had just come through the 2008-09 bailout and bonus controversies. Blocking the bill preserved their freedom to set executive pay without Justice Department involvement.

Subpoena power over compensation contracts and authority to void pay arrangements would have created a new enforcement regime around executive pay, reducing demand for the structuring work that goes into bonus and incentive packages. Not a primary driver of the outcome, but the bill's subpoena and contract-review provisions targeted their client work.
